rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: Explain the formation of depletion region in a p-n junction.
rows.solution:
A p-n junction is a single crystal, one half doped p-type and the other n-type, so that the two regions meet at a plane. The depletion region forms there of its own accord, before any voltage is applied.

**The diffusion.** The p-side is rich in holes and the n-side rich in electrons, so across the junction there is a steep concentration gradient in both carriers. Each diffuses down its own gradient: **electrons diffuse from the n-side into the p-side, and holes from the p-side into the n-side.** They recombine on arrival, so near the junction the mobile carriers are removed.

**What is left behind.** The dopant ions themselves are fixed in the crystal lattice and cannot move. An electron leaving the n-side strands a positively charged **donor** ion there; a hole leaving the p-side strands a negatively charged **acceptor** ion. So a layer builds up carrying immobile positive charge on the n-side of the junction and immobile negative charge on the p-side. Because this layer is emptied of mobile carriers it is called the **depletion region**, and it is typically a fraction of a micrometre wide.

**Why it stops growing.** These fixed charges set up an electric field directed **from the n-side towards the p-side** — that is, opposing the very diffusion that created them. Each further carrier that tries to cross must now work against this field. As the layer widens the field strengthens, until diffusion is exactly balanced by the drift it drives in the opposite direction. At that point the net current is zero and the width becomes steady.

The potential difference established across the layer is the **barrier potential** — about \(0{\cdot}3\) V for germanium and \(0{\cdot}7\) V for silicon. It cannot be measured with a voltmeter across the terminals of an isolated diode, since equal and opposite contact potentials appear at the two metal contacts, but it is exactly what an applied forward voltage has to overcome before the diode conducts.

rows.stem:
(i) Define the terms : 'impact parameter' and 'distance of closest approach' for an \(\alpha\)-particle in Geiger-Marsden scattering experiment.
(ii) What will be the value of the impact parameter for scattering angle (I) \(\theta = 0^\circ\) and (II) \(\theta = 180^\circ\) ?
rows.solution:
**(i) The two terms.**

**Impact parameter** \(b\): the perpendicular distance from the centre of the target nucleus to the line along which the alpha particle was originally travelling. It is the miss-distance the particle would have if there were no force between them, and it decides how violently the particle is deflected.

**Distance of closest approach** \(d\): the least distance to which an alpha particle fired *directly at* a nucleus gets before its motion is reversed. At that point it has come momentarily to rest, its entire kinetic energy having been converted into electrostatic potential energy:

\(K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(2e)(Ze)}{d} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2Ze^{2}}{K}\)

**(ii) Values of the impact parameter.**

**(I) For \(\theta = 0^\circ\):** \(b\) is **maximum**. A particle that passes far from the nucleus feels almost no force and carries straight on. The largest useful value of \(b\) is of the order of the atomic radius, beyond which the nucleus is screened by the atomic electrons.

**(II) For \(\theta = 180^\circ\):** \(b\) is **minimum, and equal to zero**. Only a particle aimed exactly at the centre — a head-on collision — can be turned right back along its own path.

The relation between them is monotonic: the smaller the impact parameter, the closer the approach and the larger the deflection. That is precisely why so few particles scatter through large angles — a small \(b\) means a small target area, and the number of particles with impact parameter less than \(b\) scales as \(b^{2}\). The rarity of backscattering is therefore a direct measure of how small the nucleus is, and it is the distance of closest approach at \(\theta = 180^\circ\) that sets an upper bound on the nuclear radius.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: Photoelectric emission occurs when a surface is irradiated with the radiation of frequency (i) \(v_1\), and (ii) \(v_2\). The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons emitted in the two cases are K and 2K respectively. Obtain the expression for the threshold frequency for the surface.
rows.solution:
Apply Einstein's photoelectric equation to each case, with the same surface and therefore the same threshold frequency \(\nu_0\):

\(K = h\nu_1 - \phi_0 \qquad \text{...(1)}\)

\(2K = h\nu_2 - \phi_0 \qquad \text{...(2)}\)

Multiplying (1) by 2 and setting it equal to (2):

\(2(h\nu_1 - \phi_0) = h\nu_2 - \phi_0\)

\(2h\nu_1 - 2\phi_0 = h\nu_2 - \phi_0\)

\(2h\nu_1 - h\nu_2 = \phi_0\)

\(h(2\nu_1 - \nu_2) = \phi_0\)

Since the work function can be written as \(\phi_0 = h\nu_0\), the factor \(h\) cancels:

\(\nu_0 = 2\nu_1 - \nu_2\)

That is the threshold frequency for the surface.

Two checks on the form. It must be *lower* than either applied frequency, and it is: since \(2K > K\) we need \(\nu_2 > \nu_1\), so \(2\nu_1 - \nu_2 < \nu_1\). And it has the right character — a difference of two measured frequencies, requiring neither \(h\) nor the work function in joules. This is in fact how the threshold frequency is determined experimentally: measure the stopping potential at two frequencies and extrapolate, without needing to know \(h\) at all.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: How is an emf generated by a solar cell due to the three basic processes involved ? Explain.
rows.solution:
A solar cell is a p-n junction with a very thin, transparent top layer so that light can reach the junction region. It is operated with **no external bias**; the light itself generates the emf, through three processes in sequence.

**(i) Generation.** Photons of energy \(h\nu > E_g\) are absorbed in or very near the depletion region, each lifting an electron across the band gap and so creating an **electron–hole pair**. The junction must lie close to the illuminated surface, or the pairs are created too far away to be collected.

**(ii) Separation.** The depletion region already carries the built-in electric field, directed from the n-side to the p-side. This field acts on the newly created pair and sweeps the two carriers in opposite directions — **electrons towards the n-side, holes towards the p-side** — before they can recombine. This is the crucial step: without a field to separate them, the pair would simply recombine and the energy would be lost as heat.

**(iii) Collection.** The electrons arriving on the n-side are gathered by the front contact, and the holes arriving on the p-side by the back contact.

**The resulting emf.** Charge therefore accumulates with the **p-side positive and the n-side negative**, and this separation of charge is the photovoltage appearing across the terminals. Connecting a load lets the carriers return through the external circuit, delivering current.

Note the direction: the photo-generated current inside the cell flows from n to p, opposite to the forward current of an ordinary diode, which is why a solar cell operates in the fourth quadrant of the diode characteristic and delivers power rather than consuming it.

rows.stem:
(i) Depict a plane electromagnetic wave propagating along the x-axis. Write the expressions for its oscillating electric and magnetic fields.
(ii) Write three characteristics of electromagnetic waves.
rows.solution:
**(i) A plane electromagnetic wave along the x-axis.**

*The picture.* Draw the \(x\)-axis as the direction of propagation. The electric field oscillates sinusoidally in the \(y\)-direction and the magnetic field sinusoidally in the \(z\)-direction, the two **in phase** with each other — both peaking, and both vanishing, at the same points along the wave. The three directions form a right-handed set, with \(\vec{E} \times \vec{B}\) pointing along \(+x\).

*The expressions.*

\(E_y = E_0\sin(kx - \omega t)\)

\(B_z = B_0\sin(kx - \omega t)\)

with the same \(k\) and \(\omega\) in both, and their amplitudes linked by \(B_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{c}\).

**(ii) Three characteristics of electromagnetic waves.**

- **They are transverse.** Both \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B}\) oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation, and perpendicular to each other. This is what makes light capable of being polarised.

- **They travel at the speed of light in vacuum**, \(c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and **require no material medium** — they propagate through vacuum, unlike sound or waves on a string.

- **They carry energy and momentum.** The energy is shared equally between the electric and magnetic fields, and the momentum delivered is what produces radiation pressure.

(They are also undeviated by electric or magnetic fields, being uncharged, and their speed in a medium falls to \(c/\mu\) while their frequency stays fixed.)

rows.stem:
Name the electromagnetic waves which are produced by the following :
(i) Radioactive decays of nucleus
(ii) Welding arcs
(iii) Hot bodies
Write one use each of these waves.
rows.solution:
**(i) Radioactive decay of a nucleus — gamma rays.**

Produced when an excited daughter nucleus drops to a lower nuclear energy level, emitting the surplus as a photon. These are the shortest wavelengths known, below about \(10^{-12}\) m.

*Use:* radiotherapy, in which the beam is directed at a tumour to destroy malignant cells. (They are also used to sterilise surgical instruments and food.)

**(ii) Welding arcs — ultraviolet rays.**

The arc reaches temperatures of several thousand kelvin, hot enough for its thermal radiation to peak in the ultraviolet. This is exactly why welders wear dark visors: the UV would otherwise burn the cornea.

*Use:* sterilising drinking water and surgical equipment, UV lamps destroying bacteria by damaging their DNA. (Also in the detection of forged banknotes and documents.)

**(iii) Hot bodies — infrared rays.**

Any body above absolute zero radiates, and for bodies at ordinary temperatures the emission peaks in the infrared — which is why infrared is often called heat radiation.

*Use:* night-vision cameras and thermal imaging, which form a picture from the infrared a warm body emits and so need no illumination at all. (Also in remote controls and in physiotherapy.)

The three fall at widely separated points of the spectrum, and each is characteristic of the energy scale of its source: nuclear transitions release MeV, so gamma; the arc's atomic transitions release a few eV, so ultraviolet; and a merely warm body's thermal energy is a fraction of an eV, so infrared. (The marking scheme accepts the neighbouring bands for the arc, the boundaries between named regions being conventions rather than sharp divisions.)

rows.stem:
(a) State the conditions for total internal reflection to take place.
(b) A tank is filled with a transparent liquid to height 'H'. A coin suspended by a thread in the liquid is gradually lowered till it touches the bottom. The apparent depth is determined corresponding to different positions of the coin.
(i) Plot a graph showing variation of the apparent depth with the real depth of the coin.
(ii) What is the physical significance of the slope of the graph ?
rows.solution:
**(a) Conditions for total internal reflection.**

Two conditions must both be met:

**(i)** The light must be travelling from an **optically denser medium into a rarer one** — that is, from higher refractive index to lower.

**(ii)** The **angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle** for that pair of media, where

\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{n_{\text{rarer}}}{n_{\text{denser}}}\)

If either fails, some light is refracted out and the reflection is only partial.

**(b)(i) Apparent depth against real depth.**

For an object viewed normally from above,

\(\text{apparent depth} = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\mu}\)

Since \(\mu\) is a constant of the liquid, this is a **straight line through the origin**, of constant positive slope less than 1. As the coin is lowered from the surface to the bottom, both depths increase together in fixed proportion, so the plot is linear all the way.

The line passes through the origin because a coin at the surface has zero real depth and appears at zero depth too, and its slope is less than 1 because the apparent depth is always the smaller of the two.

**(b)(ii) Significance of the slope.**

Rearranging,

\(\text{slope} = \dfrac{\text{apparent depth}}{\text{real depth}} = \dfrac{1}{\mu}\)

so the slope is the **reciprocal of the refractive index of the liquid**. Measuring it gives \(\mu\) directly, as \(\mu = 1/\text{slope}\).

This is the physical content of the experiment: it turns a refractive index into a slope, which can be read off many measurements at once rather than from a single pair of depths, and so averages out the error in any one of them.

rows.stem: Draw a labelled ray diagram showing the formation of an image by an astronomical refracting telescope in normal adjustment. Hence, obtain the expression for its magnifying power.
rows.solution:
**The ray diagram.** An objective lens of long focal length \(f_o\) and an eyepiece of short focal length \(f_e\) are mounted coaxially. Parallel rays from a distant object, arriving at a small angle \(\alpha\) to the axis, are brought to a focus by the objective, forming a **real, inverted, diminished image** \(A'B'\) of height \(h\) in its focal plane.

In **normal adjustment** the eyepiece is positioned so that this image lies at *its* focal point too — the two focal planes coincide. The eyepiece therefore sends out parallel light, and the final image is formed **at infinity**, where a relaxed eye can view it without accommodation. The separation of the lenses is \(f_o + f_e\), which is the tube length.

**Deriving the magnifying power.**

Magnifying power is the ratio of the angle \(\beta\) subtended at the eye by the final image to the angle \(\alpha\) subtended by the object at the unaided eye. Since the object is distant, \(\alpha\) is also the angle it subtends at the objective:

\(m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} \approx \dfrac{\tan\beta}{\tan\alpha}\)

(valid because both angles are small).

From the geometry, the intermediate image of height \(h\) sits a distance \(f_o\) from the objective and a distance \(f_e\) from the eyepiece:

\(\tan\alpha = \dfrac{h}{f_o}, \qquad \tan\beta = \dfrac{h}{f_e}\)

Hence

\(m = \dfrac{h/f_e}{h/f_o} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\)

The intermediate height \(h\) cancels, which is why the result depends only on the two focal lengths.

**The design that follows.** High magnification needs a **long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece** — the opposite of a compound microscope, where both must be short. It also explains why refracting telescopes are physically long instruments: the tube must be about \(f_o\), and \(f_o\) is what the magnification is made of. The conventional minus sign, \(m = -f_o/f_e\), simply records that the image is inverted.

rows.stem:
A plane wavefront of light of wavelength '\(\lambda\)' is incident normally on a narrow slit of width 'a' and a diffraction pattern is observed on a screen at a distance 'D' from the slit.
(i) Depict the intensity distribution in the pattern observed.
(ii) Obtain the expression for the first maximum from the central maximum.
rows.solution:
**(i) The intensity distribution.**

Plot intensity against the diffraction angle \(\theta\). The pattern consists of:

- a **central maximum** at \(\theta = 0\), twice as wide as any other band and overwhelmingly the brightest, running between the first minima on either side;
- **minima** at \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{n\lambda}{a}\) for \(n = \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \ldots\) — note \(n = 0\) is excluded, since that is the central maximum;
- **secondary maxima** roughly midway between consecutive minima, falling off rapidly in brightness — the first is only about 4·7% of the central peak, the second about 1·7%.

So the curve is a tall central peak flanked by progressively fainter, equally spaced subsidiary peaks that decay away on both sides.

**(ii) Position of the first secondary maximum.**

The secondary maxima occur where the path difference across the slit is an odd number of half-wavelengths, the extra half-wavelength being what survives after the rest of the slit cancels in pairs:

\(a\sin\theta = \left(n + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda\)

For the **first** secondary maximum, \(n = 1\):

\(a\sin\theta = \dfrac{3\lambda}{2}\)

For small angles \(\sin\theta \approx \theta \approx \dfrac{x}{D}\), where \(x\) is the distance from the central maximum on a screen at distance \(D\):

\(a \times \dfrac{x}{D} = \dfrac{3\lambda}{2}\)

\(x = \dfrac{3\lambda D}{2a}\)

Comparing with the first minimum at \(\lambda D / a\) shows the structure of the pattern: the central bright band is \(2\lambda D/a\) wide, and the first secondary peak sits halfway between the first and second minima, at one and a half times the half-width of the central band.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem:
A converging lens made of glass (\(\mu = 1{\cdot}5\)) has its spherical faces of radii of curvature 10 cm and 20 cm. Find its focal length
(a) in air, and
(b) when it is immersed in a liquid of refractive index \(1{\cdot}25\).
rows.solution:
The lens-maker's formula, written for a lens in a surrounding medium, handles both parts:

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{\mu_{\text{lens}}}{\mu_{\text{medium}}} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\)

Since the lens is converging with faces of radii 10 cm and 20 cm, it is biconvex: \(R_1 = +10\) cm and \(R_2 = -20\) cm. The geometrical bracket is therefore the same in both parts:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{-20} = \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{3}{20}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

**(a) In air**, \(\mu_{\text{medium}} = 1\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f_a} = (1{\cdot}5 - 1)\left(\dfrac{3}{20}\right) = 0{\cdot}5 \times \dfrac{3}{20} = \dfrac{3}{40}\)

\(f_a = \dfrac{40}{3} = 13{\cdot}3\ \text{cm}\)

**(b) In the liquid**, \(\mu_{\text{medium}} = 1{\cdot}25\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f_l} = \left(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{1{\cdot}25} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{20}\right) = (1{\cdot}2 - 1) \times \dfrac{3}{20} = 0{\cdot}2 \times \dfrac{3}{20} = \dfrac{3}{100}\)

\(f_l = \dfrac{100}{3} = 33{\cdot}3\ \text{cm}\)

**The focal length has grown by a factor of \(2{\cdot}5\)** — the lens is two and a half times weaker in the liquid, though still converging.

The reason is that refraction depends on the *contrast* in refractive index, not on the lens's index alone. Immersing the lens reduces that contrast from \(0{\cdot}5\) to \(0{\cdot}2\), and the power falls in proportion. Taken further, a lens immersed in a liquid of its own refractive index would have \(f \to \infty\) and vanish optically altogether; in a liquid *denser* than the glass, the bracket would go negative and the converging lens would begin to diverge.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem:
The energy of a hydrogen atom in the first excited state is \(-\,3{\cdot}4\) eV. Find :
(a) the radius of this orbit. (Take Bohr radius = \(0{\cdot}53\) Å)
(b) the angular momentum of the electron in the orbit.
(c) the kinetic and potential energy of the electron in the orbit.
rows.solution:
The first excited state is \(n = 2\), and the given energy \(-3{\cdot}4\) eV confirms it: \(E_n = -13{\cdot}6/n^{2}\) gives \(-13{\cdot}6/4 = -3{\cdot}4\) eV.

**(a) Radius of the orbit.**

In the Bohr model \(r_n = n^{2}r_0\), with \(r_0 = 0{\cdot}53\) Å the Bohr radius:

\(r_2 = (2)^{2} \times 0{\cdot}53 = 2{\cdot}12\ \text{Å} = 2{\cdot}12 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}\)

**(b) Angular momentum.**

Bohr's quantisation condition gives

\(L = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi} = \dfrac{2 \times 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{2 \times 3{\cdot}14}\)

\(L = 2{\cdot}11 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\)

(the unit being J s, equivalently \(\mathrm{kg\,m^{2}\,s^{-1}}\)).

**(c) Kinetic and potential energy.**

For a Coulomb bound state the virial theorem fixes both in terms of the total energy:

\(K = -E \qquad\text{and}\qquad U = 2E\)

So with \(E = -3{\cdot}4\) eV:

\(K = +3{\cdot}4\ \text{eV}, \qquad U = -6{\cdot}8\ \text{eV}\)

These follow directly rather than needing separate calculation. The electrostatic attraction supplies the centripetal force, \(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{ke^{2}}{r^{2}}\), so \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{ke^{2}}{2r}\) while \(U = -\dfrac{ke^{2}}{r} = -2K\). Adding gives \(E = K + U = -K\), which is the relation used above.

The signs carry the physics: \(U\) is negative and twice the magnitude of \(K\), so the total energy is negative and the electron is **bound**. Supplying \(3{\cdot}4\) eV would free it from this level — the ionisation energy from the first excited state.

rows.stem:
(a) Depict the variation of the potential energy of a pair of nucleons with the separation between them.
(b) Imagine the fission of a \({}^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}\) into two equal fragments of \({}^{28}_{13}\mathrm{Al}\) nucleus. Is the fission energetically possible ? Justify your answer by working out Q value of the process.
Given : \(m\left({}^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}\right) = 55{\cdot}93494\) u, \(m\left({}^{28}_{13}\mathrm{Al}\right) = 27{\cdot}98191\) u.
rows.solution:
**(a) Potential energy of a pair of nucleons against their separation.**

Plot potential energy (in MeV) against separation \(r\) (in fm). The curve has three distinct regions:

- For \(r\) greater than about 0·8 fm the potential is **negative** — attractive — rising towards zero as \(r\) increases and becoming negligible beyond about 3 fm. This short range is the defining feature of the nuclear force.
- The curve passes through a **minimum of about \(-100\) MeV at \(r_0 \approx 0{\cdot}8\) fm**, the separation of greatest stability.
- Below \(r_0\) the potential energy climbs **very steeply into large positive values** — the force becomes strongly **repulsive**, which is what stops nuclear matter from collapsing and keeps nuclei at an almost constant density.

The curve crosses zero at \(r = r_0\) on the way up, so the force (the negative gradient) is attractive outside \(r_0\), zero at \(r_0\) and repulsive within it.

**(b) Is the fission of iron-56 into two aluminium-28 nuclei possible?**

\({}^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe} \longrightarrow 2\,{}^{28}_{13}\mathrm{Al}\)

The bookkeeping checks out: \(56 = 2 \times 28\) and \(26 = 2 \times 13\).

**Mass difference:**

\(\Delta m = m({}^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}) - 2\,m({}^{28}_{13}\mathrm{Al})\)

\(2 \times 27{\cdot}98191 = 55{\cdot}96382\)

\(\Delta m = 55{\cdot}93494 - 55{\cdot}96382 = -0{\cdot}02888\ \text{u}\)

**Q value:**

\(Q = \Delta m \times 931{\cdot}5 = -0{\cdot}02888 \times 931{\cdot}5 = -26{\cdot}9\ \text{MeV}\)

**The fission is not energetically possible.** The products are *heavier* than the parent, so energy would have to be supplied rather than released — about 27 MeV of it. A process with a negative Q value cannot occur spontaneously.

(The marking scheme prints the mass difference as \(-0{\cdot}02442\) u; its own two figures give \(55{\cdot}93494 - 55{\cdot}96382 = -0{\cdot}02888\) u. Both are negative, so the verdict is unaffected, but the scheme stops at the mass difference without converting to the Q value the question asks for.)

**Why it had to come out this way.** Iron-56 sits at the very peak of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve, more tightly bound per nucleon than any other nucleus. Splitting it necessarily moves its nucleons *down* the curve to a less tightly bound configuration, which costs energy. This is exactly why fission releases energy only for nuclei much heavier than iron, and fusion only for nuclei much lighter — and why stellar nucleosynthesis stops at iron.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem:
Find the ratio of the de Broglie wavelengths associated with an alpha particle and a proton, if both
(a) have the same speeds,
(b) have the same kinetic energy,
(c) are accelerated through the same potential difference.
rows.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\), so each part turns on expressing the momentum in terms of the quantity held fixed. Throughout, \(m_\alpha = 4m_p\) and \(q_\alpha = 2q_p\).

**(a) Same speed.** Here \(p = mv\) with \(v\) common:

\(\dfrac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_p} = \dfrac{h/(m_\alpha v)}{h/(m_p v)} = \dfrac{m_p}{m_\alpha} = \dfrac{1}{4}\)

**(b) Same kinetic energy.** Here \(p = \sqrt{2mK}\) with \(K\) common:

\(\dfrac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p}{m_\alpha}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

**(c) Same accelerating potential.** Now \(K = qV\), so \(p = \sqrt{2mqV}\) with \(V\) common:

\(\dfrac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p q_p}{m_\alpha q_\alpha}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4 \times 2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{8}} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\)

**The three answers — \(\dfrac{1}{4}\), \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\) — are all different**, and the pattern is worth reading off. The mass ratio enters to the first power in (a), to the half power in (b), and to the half power again in (c) but with the charge ratio joining it. Each condition holds a different quantity fixed, so each weights the mass difference differently, and quoting one answer for another is the mistake the question is built to catch.

Note also that \(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \approx 0{\cdot}354\) lies between the other two, as it must: accelerating through the same potential gives the alpha particle twice the energy of the proton, which is a smaller advantage than the equal-speed case but larger than equal energy.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem: With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of a p-n junction diode as a full-wave rectifier. Also draw its input and output waveforms.
rows.solution:
**The circuit.** A **centre-tap transformer** supplies the input. Its secondary is tapped at the midpoint, and the two ends, A and B, are connected to the anodes of diodes \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) respectively. The cathodes of both diodes are joined and connected through the load resistance \(R_L\) back to the centre tap.

The essential property of the centre tap is that the voltages at A and B, measured with respect to it, are always **equal in magnitude and opposite in sign**. At every instant one end is positive and the other negative.

**Working.**

*Positive half-cycle.* Suppose A is positive with respect to the centre tap. Then B is negative. \(D_1\) is forward biased and conducts, while \(D_2\) is reverse biased and does not. Current flows from A, through \(D_1\), down through \(R_L\), and back to the centre tap.

*Negative half-cycle.* Now A is negative and B positive. \(D_1\) stops conducting and \(D_2\) takes over. Current flows from B, through \(D_2\), and then **through \(R_L\) in the same direction as before**, back to the centre tap.

That last point is the whole mechanism. The two diodes are fed from opposite ends of the secondary but both deliver current to the load from the same side, so reversing the source does not reverse the current in the load. The two diodes conduct in alternate half-cycles and neither is ever idle for long.

**Waveforms.**

*Input:* an ordinary sinusoid, alternating above and below the time axis.

*Output across \(R_L\):* a succession of positive half-sinusoids with **no gaps between them** — one from \(D_1\), the next from \(D_2\), then \(D_1\) again, and so on. The negative half of each input cycle has been folded up rather than discarded.

Compared with a half-wave rectifier, the output delivers twice the average voltage and its ripple is at **twice the input frequency**, which a given smoothing capacitor filters far more effectively. That doubled ripple frequency is the practical reason full-wave rectification is preferred.

rows.stem: If the screen is moved closer to the plane of slits \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\), then the fringe width :
rows.context: The British physicist Thomas Young explained the interference of light using the principle of superposition of waves. He observed the interference pattern on the screen, in his experimental set-up, known now as Young's double slit experiment. The two slits \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) were illuminated by light from a slit S. The interference pattern consists of dark and bright bands of light. Such bands are called fringes. The distance between two consecutive bright and dark fringes is called fringe width.

options.label: A
options.text: will decrease, but the intensity of bright fringe remains the same.

options.label: B
options.text: will increase, but the intensity of bright fringe decreases.

options.label: C
options.text: will decrease, but the intensity of bright fringe increases.

options.label: D
options.text: and the intensity both remain the same.

rows.solution:
Two separate quantities change, and they change in opposite directions.

**Fringe width.** \(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\). Moving the screen closer reduces \(D\), so the fringe width **decreases** — the whole pattern shrinks.

**Intensity of a bright fringe.** The same total light energy leaving the slits now falls on a smaller area of screen, since the pattern has contracted. Energy per unit area therefore **increases**, so each bright fringe is brighter.

So the fringe width decreases while the intensity increases — option (C).

The two effects are linked rather than independent: the pattern is a fixed set of *directions* determined by \(\lambda\) and \(d\), and moving the screen merely changes how far the light has spread before it is intercepted. Nearer means less spread, hence narrower fringes and more light concentrated in each. (This is also why the *angular* fringe separation, \(\lambda/d\), does not change at all when the screen is moved — only the linear width does.)

rows.stem: What will happen to the pattern on the screen, when the two slits \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) are replaced by two independent but identical sources ?
rows.context: The British physicist Thomas Young explained the interference of light using the principle of superposition of waves. He observed the interference pattern on the screen, in his experimental set-up, known now as Young's double slit experiment. The two slits \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) were illuminated by light from a slit S. The interference pattern consists of dark and bright bands of light. Such bands are called fringes. The distance between two consecutive bright and dark fringes is called fringe width.

options.label: A
options.text: The intensity of pattern will increase

options.label: B
options.text: The intensity of pattern will decrease

options.label: C
options.text: The number of fringes will become double

options.label: D
options.text: No pattern will be observed on the screen

rows.solution:
Sustained interference requires the two sources to be **coherent** — to maintain a constant phase difference over the time of observation. In Young's experiment this is guaranteed by construction: \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are two slits illuminated by the *same* wavefront from a single source, so any phase fluctuation at the source reaches both slits together and the difference between them never changes.

Two **independent** sources cannot do this, however identical they are made. Light is emitted in short, random wave trains lasting about \(10^{-9}\) s, with the phase resetting at random between them. The phase difference between two independent sources therefore changes randomly millions of times per second.

The pattern of maxima and minima consequently shifts about far faster than the eye or any detector can follow, and what is observed is the **time average** — a uniform illumination equal to the plain sum \(I_1 + I_2\), with no fringes anywhere.

So **no pattern will be observed on the screen**, option (D).

Being "identical" is not the same as being coherent: identical sources have the same wavelength and amplitude, but nothing ties their phases together. This is why interference could not be demonstrated with two separate lamps for over a century, and why lasers — whose emission stays coherent for far longer — changed what the experiment could be done with.

rows.stem: Two sources of light are said to be coherent, when both emit light waves of :
rows.context: The British physicist Thomas Young explained the interference of light using the principle of superposition of waves. He observed the interference pattern on the screen, in his experimental set-up, known now as Young's double slit experiment. The two slits \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) were illuminated by light from a slit S. The interference pattern consists of dark and bright bands of light. Such bands are called fringes. The distance between two consecutive bright and dark fringes is called fringe width.

options.label: A
options.text: same amplitude and have a varying phase difference.

options.label: B
options.text: same wavelength and a constant phase difference.

options.label: C
options.text: different wavelengths and same intensity.

options.label: D
options.text: different wavelengths and a constant phase difference.

rows.solution:
Two sources are coherent when they emit waves of the **same wavelength (hence the same frequency) with a constant phase difference** between them — option (B).

Both conditions are necessary, and each fails differently.

If the **wavelengths differ**, the phase difference between the two waves at any fixed point drifts steadily with time, at a rate set by the frequency difference. Whatever pattern forms sweeps across the screen and averages away.

If the wavelengths match but the **phase difference varies**, the positions of the maxima wander randomly, and again the time average is a uniform illumination.

Note what is *not* required: the amplitudes need not be equal. Unequal amplitudes still give interference, just with imperfect contrast — the minima are no longer completely dark, since \(I_{\min} = \left(\sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2}\right)^{2}\) is zero only when the two intensities are equal. Amplitude affects the *visibility* of the fringes; coherence decides whether there are any fringes at all.

rows.stem: The fringe width in a Young's double slit experiment is \(\beta\). If the whole set-up is immersed in a liquid of refractive index '\(\mu\)', then the new fringe width will be :
rows.context: The British physicist Thomas Young explained the interference of light using the principle of superposition of waves. He observed the interference pattern on the screen, in his experimental set-up, known now as Young's double slit experiment. The two slits \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) were illuminated by light from a slit S. The interference pattern consists of dark and bright bands of light. Such bands are called fringes. The distance between two consecutive bright and dark fringes is called fringe width.

options.label: A
options.text: \(\beta\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(\beta\mu\)

options.label: C
options.text: \(\dfrac{\beta}{\mu}\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(\dfrac{\beta}{\mu^2}\)

rows.solution:
Immersing the whole arrangement changes the wavelength of the light, and nothing else in the fringe-width formula.

The frequency of light is fixed by the source and cannot change at a boundary, but the speed falls to \(v = c/\mu\), so the wavelength shortens:

\(\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{\mu}\)

The slit separation \(d\) and the screen distance \(D\) are physical lengths and are unaffected. So

\(\beta' = \dfrac{\lambda' D}{d} = \dfrac{\lambda D}{\mu d} = \dfrac{\beta}{\mu}\)

The new fringe width is \(\dfrac{\beta}{\mu}\), option (C).

Since \(\mu > 1\) for any liquid, the fringes move **closer together** — the pattern contracts by exactly the refractive index. Only one power of \(\mu\) appears, which rules out the \(\beta/\mu^{2}\) option: the wavelength enters the fringe-width formula linearly, so a single factor is all that can be picked up.

rows.stem: The total path difference between two waves meeting at points \(\mathrm{P_1}\) and \(\mathrm{P_2}\) on the screen are \(\left(\dfrac{3\lambda}{2}\right)\) and \(2\lambda\) respectively. Then :
rows.context: The British physicist Thomas Young explained the interference of light using the principle of superposition of waves. He observed the interference pattern on the screen, in his experimental set-up, known now as Young's double slit experiment. The two slits \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) were illuminated by light from a slit S. The interference pattern consists of dark and bright bands of light. Such bands are called fringes. The distance between two consecutive bright and dark fringes is called fringe width.

options.label: A
options.text: bright fringes are formed at both points.

options.label: B
options.text: dark fringes are formed at both points.

options.label: C
options.text: a bright fringe is formed at \(\mathrm{P_1}\) and a dark fringe is formed at \(\mathrm{P_2}\).

options.label: D
options.text: a bright fringe is formed at \(\mathrm{P_2}\) and a dark fringe is formed at \(\mathrm{P_1}\).

rows.solution:
Classify each point by how many wavelengths of path difference it carries.

**At \(P_1\):** \(\Delta x = \dfrac{3\lambda}{2}\). This is an **odd multiple of a half-wavelength**, \((2n-1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\) with \(n = 2\). The two waves arrive exactly out of phase, they cancel, and a **dark fringe** is formed.

**At \(P_2\):** \(\Delta x = 2\lambda\). This is a **whole number of wavelengths**, \(n\lambda\) with \(n = 2\). The two waves arrive in phase, they reinforce, and a **bright fringe** is formed.

So a bright fringe at \(P_2\) and a dark fringe at \(P_1\) — option (D).

The test is quick once the path difference is read as a multiple of \(\lambda\): whole numbers give maxima, half-odd numbers give minima. Expressed as phase, \(\Delta x = 3\lambda/2\) corresponds to \(\phi = 3\pi\), which is equivalent to \(\pi\), while \(\Delta x = 2\lambda\) corresponds to \(\phi = 4\pi\), equivalent to zero. The options are arranged so that reading \(3\lambda/2\) as "one and a half, so partly bright" leads to the wrong pair — but interference has no partial case at a given point, only the full constructive or destructive result.
